title_en: Bl’s David Cohne on Lessons From Active Managers
title_zh: Bloomberg 的 David Cohne 谈从主动管理型基金经理身上学到的经验
subtitle_zh: David Cohne 独自复盘：如何区分可复制的投资流程与恰好被市场奖励的好故事。
description: Bl’s David Cohne on Lessons From Active Managers

turns.en: For big business, AI opened up a world of promise, but that world of promise turned into a world of pain, cost spiraling data-trapped security and governance risks, multiplying, and ROI out of reach. That's why enterprises turned to Boomi to connect data, apps, and AI, helping them operate securely, efficiently, and at scale.
turns.zh: 对大型企业来说，AI 打开了一片充满希望的世界，可这片希望之地却变成了痛苦之地——成本不断飙升、数据被困在孤岛里、安全与治理风险层层叠加，投资回报（ROI）遥不可及。正因如此，企业纷纷转向 Boomi，用它把数据、应用和 AI 连接起来，帮助它们安全、高效、大规模地运转。

turns.en: Boomi turns a world of AI pain into a world of AI gain. As Boomi says, we got you head to boomi.com. That's B-O-O-M-I-DOT-COM. [♪ OUTRO MUSIC PLAYING [♪ Welcome to Inside Active, a podcast about active managers that goes beyond sound bites and headlines and looks deeper into their processes, challenges, and philosophies
turns.zh: Boomi 把 AI 的痛苦世界变成 AI 的收获世界。就像 Boomi 说的：这事包在我们身上——欢迎访问 boomi.com，也就是 B-O-O-M-I 点 COM。[♪ 片尾音乐播放中 [♪ 欢迎收听 Inside Active，这是一档关于主动管理型基金经理（active managers）的播客，我们不满足于只言片语和头条标题，而是更深入地去剖析他们的投资流程、面临的挑战、投资理念

turns.en: and security selection. I'm David Cohn, I lead Mutual Fund and Active Research at Bloomberg Intelligence. So we're doing something a little different on the podcast this week. Usually I'm joined by a portfolio manager or someone else from the industry, but after spending the past couple of years talking with active managers on the podcast
turns.zh: 以及选股（security selection）之道。我是 David Cohne，在 Bloomberg Intelligence 负责共同基金与主动管理研究（Mutual Fund and Active Research）。这周我们在播客里要做点不太一样的事。平时我都会请来一位投资组合经理（portfolio manager）或者业内的其他嘉宾，但在过去几年里，我在这档播客上和众多主动管理型基金经理聊过之后，

turns.en: about how they invest, I thought it would be interesting to take a step back and talk about some of the things I've learned from those conversations and also how they line up with what I'm seeing in my own research. One of the reasons I started this podcast was that there was a lot we can learn about a fund from the numbers.
turns.zh: 聊他们是怎么做投资的，我觉得不妨退后一步，谈谈我从这些对话里学到的一些东西，也谈谈它们和我在自己研究中看到的情况是否吻合。我当初做这档播客的原因之一，就是：关于一只基金，我们能从数据里读到很多东西。

turns.en: We can look at performance, holdings, fees, risk, factor exposure, and flows. But those numbers don't necessarily tell us why a manager owns what they own, what they think their edges, or whether that edge has a reasonable chance of persisting. That's what I've tried to understand through these conversations.
turns.zh: 我们可以看业绩、持仓、费率、风险、因子暴露（factor exposure）和资金流（flows）。但这些数字未必能告诉我们：一位经理为什么持有他手里的这些标的、他认为自己的优势（edge）在哪里，以及这种优势有没有合理的机会持续下去。而这些，正是我想通过这些对话去弄明白的东西。

turns.en: And after talking with managers who invest very differently from one another, I found myself coming back to a few questions. How do you distinguish a repeatable investment process from one that is simply benefited from the right market environment? How much can past performance really tell us about manager skill?
turns.zh: 在和一群投资风格彼此差异极大的经理聊过之后，我发现自己反复回到几个问题上。你怎么区分一套可复制的投资流程，和一套只是恰好受益于合适市场环境的流程？过往业绩到底能在多大程度上告诉我们一位经理的真实本事（skill）？

turns.en: What should we look for when we're trying to determine whether an active manager actually has an edge? And maybe most importantly, what does it even mean to say that active management works? So I thought I'd spend some time talking through those questions starting with investment process. If you listen to enough portfolio managers,
turns.zh: 当我们想判断一位主动管理型经理到底有没有优势时，应该留意哪些东西？也许最重要的是，说“主动管理（active management）行得通”到底是什么意思？所以我想花点时间把这些问题逐个聊一聊，先从投资流程说起。如果你听过足够多的投资组合经理讲话，

turns.en: you'll hear certain words quite a bit. Long-term quality, competitive advantage, management, valuation, discipline. And none of those things are bad. In fact, they're all important. But one thing I've learned from doing these interviews is that the description of an investment philosophy is usually much less interesting
turns.zh: 你会发现有些词被反复提到：长期（long-term）、质量（quality）、竞争优势（competitive advantage）、管理层（management）、估值（valuation）、纪律（discipline）。这些东西没有一样是坏的，事实上它们都很重要。但做了这么多访谈，我学到的一点是：对一套投资理念的描述，通常远不如

turns.en: than what happens when you start pushing on how that philosophy is actually implemented. Take long-term investing, almost every active manager would probably tell you they're a long-term investor, but that can mean very different things. For one manager, it might mean identifying a company that can compound earnings for a decade
turns.zh: 当你开始追问这套理念究竟是怎么落地的时候有意思。就拿长期投资来说，几乎每位主动管理型经理大概都会告诉你他是长期投资者，但这句话可以指代非常不同的东西。对一位经理来说，它可能意味着找出一家能够在十年里持续复利增长盈利的公司，

turns.en: and being willing to tolerate evaluation that looks expensive today. For another, it might mean buying an asset at a substantial discount to what they believe it's worth and being willing to wait years for that value to be recognized. And for another, it might mean accepting periods of significant underperformance
turns.zh: 并且愿意容忍它今天看上去很贵的估值（valuation）。对另一位经理来说，它可能意味着以大幅低于自己认为的内在价值的折扣买入一项资产，并愿意等上好几年，等这份价值被市场认可。而对又一位经理来说，它可能意味着接受一段明显跑输大盘的时期，

turns.en: because their investment horizon is much longer than the markets. Those are all very different approaches. So saying you're a long-term investor doesn't really tell me very much. What I increasingly wanted to know is what happens when things don't go according to plan? What would cause you to change your mind?
turns.zh: 因为他的投资期限比市场要长得多。这些都是截然不同的做法。所以，光说自己是长期投资者，其实告诉不了我太多信息。我越来越想弄明白的是：当事情没有按计划走的时候会发生什么？什么会让你改变主意？

turns.en: What information would tell you that your original thesis was wrong rather than simply early? And what would actually make you sell? I probably become more interested in sell discipline as I've done more of these interviews. It's relatively easy to tell a compelling story about why you bought a company.
turns.zh: 什么样的信息会让你意识到自己最初的判断（thesis）是错的，而不只是提早了？又有什么会真正让你卖出？做这些访谈做得越多，我对卖出纪律（sell discipline）就越感兴趣。要讲一个动听的故事、说明你为什么买入一家公司，其实相对容易。

turns.en: The company has a large addressable market that has strong management that has competitive advantage. Earnings can compound for years, but what happens after you own it? Suppose the stock rises much faster than the underlying business. Does valuation eventually matter enough to sell? Suppose the stock falls 30%,
turns.zh: 这家公司有巨大的潜在市场（addressable market）、有强悍的管理层、有竞争优势，盈利能连续多年复利增长。可当你真正持有它之后，又会发生什么？假设股价涨得远比底层业务快，估值最终会不会重要到让你卖出的地步？假设股价跌了 30%，

turns.en: is that an opportunity to buy more because a thesis hasn't changed? Or is a market telling you something you missed? Suppose the company is executing reasonably well, but another idea now has a much better risk and reward profile. Do you sell a company you still like? Those decisions tell you a lot about a process actually works.
turns.zh: 这是不是一次加仓的机会，因为你的判断逻辑并没有变？还是说市场在告诉你一些你漏掉的东西？假设这家公司经营得还不错，但另一个投资标的如今的风险回报比（risk and reward）要好得多，你会不会卖掉一家你依然喜欢的公司？这些决定，能告诉你很多关于一套流程究竟是否真正奏效的东西。

turns.en: And they also get it something else I've been thinking about quite a bit. The difference between having a good investment process and having a market environment that happens to reward that process. This has come up in some research I did on large growth managers. Growth has obviously been a difficult place
turns.zh: 它们还引出了另一件我最近想了很久的事：拥有一套好的投资流程，和恰好碰上一个奖励这套流程的市场环境，这两者之间的区别。这一点在我做的一项关于大盘成长型（large growth）经理的研究里也冒了出来。在这轮市场周期的不同阶段，成长股显然一直是主动管理很难施展的地方，

turns.en: for active management at different points in this market cycle, particularly with returns concentrated in a relatively small number of very large companies. When I look more closely at the funds that were succeeding, one characteristic stood out, momentum, among large cap growth funds,
turns.zh: 尤其是当回报高度集中在相对少数几家超大型公司身上的时候。当我更仔细地去审视那些表现成功的基金时，有一个特征格外突出——动量（momentum）。在大盘成长型基金当中，

turns.en: with more momentum exposure than the S&P 500 growth index, 56% beat the index. And when I wait those results by assets, the success rate was 84, among the funds with negative momentum exposure, zero beat. Now I don't think the conclusion from that is that managers simply buy whatever has the most momentum.
turns.zh: 动量暴露高于 S&P 500 成长指数（S&P 500 growth index）的基金里，有 56% 跑赢了该指数；而当我按资产对这些结果加权时，成功率高达 84%。而在动量暴露为负的基金中，跑赢的数量是零。当然，我并不认为由此得出的结论是：经理们只要去买动量最强的东西就行了。

turns.en: The more interesting question is what those results tell us about how we evaluate active management. Imagine a manager has a consistent process that tends to lead them toward companies with strong earnings growth and strong price momentum. Then the market enters an environment when those characteristics are heavily rewarded
turns.zh: 更有意思的问题是：这些结果对于我们该如何评价主动管理，说明了什么？想象一位经理有一套始终如一的流程，这套流程往往把他引向那些盈利增长强劲、价格动量也强劲的公司。随后市场进入了一个高度奖励这些特征的环境，

turns.en: and the manager substantially outperforms. Was that skill? Was it factor exposure? Was it the market environment? The answer may actually be all three and that's where evaluating active management gets difficult. Michael Irvalini came on inside active earlier this year to talk about skill versus luck
turns.zh: 这位经理于是大幅跑赢。这是本事（skill）吗？是因子暴露（factor exposure）吗？还是市场环境使然？答案也许三者兼有——而评价主动管理的难点，恰恰就在这里。今年早些时候，Michael Ervolini 上过 Inside Active，聊了聊本事与运气（skill versus luck）的话题，

turns.en: and that's a question that has stayed with me. We tend to use performance as evidence of skill because performance is so observable. But the outcome and the quality of the decision aren't necessarily the same thing. A good investment decision can produce a bad outcome. And a bad investment decision can produce a good outcome.
turns.zh: 这个问题一直留在我心里。我们习惯把业绩当成本事的证据，因为业绩太容易被观察到了。但结果和决策的质量，未必是同一回事。一个好的投资决策可能带来坏结果，一个坏的投资决策也可能带来好结果。

turns.en: In over short periods, it can be extremely difficult to separate the two. That's why I think understanding the process matters. But there's actually another side to this. A process can sound incredibly compelling in an interview yet still failed to produce good investment results. Every manager can explain why their approach should work.
turns.zh: 在很短的时间跨度里，要把这两者分开可能极其困难。这也是为什么我认为理解流程很重要。但这件事其实还有另一面：一套流程在访谈里可能听起来无比动听，却依然产不出好的投资结果。每位经理都能解释为什么他的方法应该奏效。

turns.en: Ultimately, it has to work. So we're consistently trying to reconnect those two things, the process and the outcome. And some of my research has produced results that have challenged assumptions about where active management should have an advantage. One example is fun size. That's a fairly intuitive argument
turns.zh: 可归根结底，它必须真的奏效。所以我们始终在努力把这两样东西重新连到一起——流程和结果。我的一些研究得出的结果，挑战了关于主动管理本应在哪里占据优势的固有假设。一个例子就是基金规模（fund size）。有一种相当符合直觉的论点，

turns.en: for why smaller funds should have an advantage. They can be more nimble. They can invest in smaller companies without worrying as much about liquidity or capacity. A position doesn't have to be enormous to make a difference to overall fun performance. A really large fund, a fund with a lot of assets,
turns.zh: 说明为什么规模较小的基金应该更有优势：它们可以更灵活，可以去投资更小的公司，而不用太担心流动性（liquidity）或容量（capacity）的问题；一笔持仓不必大到夸张，就能对整只基金的表现产生实质影响。而一只非常大的基金、一只资产规模庞大的基金，

turns.en: doesn't necessarily have those same advantages. But when I looked at fun size performance, that's actually not what I found. Funds with less than 500 million in assets only had a 6.1% beat rate across the periods I studied and generally success increased with the amount of assets the fund held.
turns.zh: 未必拥有同样的这些优势。但当我去研究基金规模与表现的关系时，发现事实其实并非如此。在我研究的各个时段里，资产低于 5 亿美元的基金，跑赢率（beat rate）只有 6.1%；而且总体而言，基金持有的资产越多，成功的概率反而越高。

turns.en: I found it fascinating because it raises a chicken and egg problem. Are larger funds more successful because scale provides advantages? For larger fund company may have more analysts, better access to management teams and more resources devoted towards research or risk management and trading. But maybe those funds are large
turns.zh: 我觉得这一点特别有意思，因为它抛出了一个“先有鸡还是先有蛋”的问题：规模更大的基金更成功，是因为规模本身带来了优势吗？比如，一家更大的基金公司可能有更多分析师、更容易接触到管理层团队，也有更多资源投入到研究、风险管理（risk management）和交易上。但也说不定，这些基金之所以规模大，

turns.en: because they were successful in the first place. Investors rewarded good managers with assets. So by the time we're measuring them, SARS may partly be evidence of previous success. And then there's another question. At what point does a scale that may reflect past success start making future success harder?
turns.zh: 恰恰是因为它们一开始就很成功——投资者用资产回报了优秀的经理。所以等到我们去衡量它们的时候，规模（scale）本身可能部分就是过往成功的证据。接着还有另一个问题：这种可能反映着过往成功的规模，到了哪个临界点，会开始让未来的成功变得更难？

turns.en: I don't think there's one answer. It probably depends enormously on what a manager owns. A large cap manager running billions of dollars faces a very different capacity constraint than a small cap manager running the same amount. But it illustrates why simple rules about active management can be misleading.
turns.zh: 我不认为有一个统一的答案。这在很大程度上取决于一位经理持有的是什么。一个管理着数十亿美元的大盘经理，面对的容量约束（capacity constraint），和一个管理着同样金额的小盘经理，是完全不同的。但这也说明了，为什么关于主动管理的那些简单法则可能会误导人。

turns.en: Small funds aren't necessarily better because they're nimble. And large funds aren't necessarily better because they have more resources. You have to understand what a manager is actually trying to do. There's another assumption about active management that I've been questioning through my research.
turns.zh: 小基金未必因为灵活就更好，大基金也未必因为资源多就更好。你得先弄明白一位经理到底想做什么。关于主动管理，还有另一个我一直通过研究在质疑的假设。

turns.en: We often hear a statistic along the lines of only a certain percentage of active funds beat their benchmarks. Now that's useful information. I use that myself. But there's something important hidden inside that calculation. If we're simply counting funds, $100 million fund and $100 billion fund each count exactly once,
turns.zh: 我们常听到这样一类统计：只有某个百分比的主动型基金能跑赢它们的基准（benchmark）。这是有用的信息，我自己也会用。但在这个计算里，藏着一些很重要的东西。如果我们只是简单地按基金只数来数，那么一只 1 亿美元的基金和一只 1000 亿美元的基金，各自都只算一次，

turns.en: that's not how investors experience the market. So I've increasingly been looking at performance on an asset-weighted basis as well. And in a number of categories, I found that the percentage of investor assets outperforming can actually be considerably higher than the percentage of funds outperforming.
turns.zh: 可这并不是投资者实际体验市场的方式。所以我越来越多地也会按资产加权（asset-weighted）的口径去看表现。在很多类别里，我发现：跑赢的投资者资产所占的百分比，其实可能明显高于跑赢的基金只数所占的百分比。

turns.en: That doesn't make the traditional success rate wrong. It's answering a different question. See, one asks, what percentage of managers succeeded? And the other is asking what percentage of the money invested with those managers experience success? And I think you actually need both because if 30% of funds beat their benchmark,
turns.zh: 这并不意味着传统的那种成功率是错的，它只是在回答一个不同的问题。你看，一个问的是：有多大比例的经理成功了？另一个问的是：投给这些经理的钱里，有多大比例获得了成功？我认为你其实两个都需要。因为如果有 30% 的基金跑赢了基准，

turns.en: but those funds hold 60% of the assets, the conclusion that 70% of active investors field isn't really accurate. And it also raises another interesting question about manager selection. We often talk about active management as though investors randomly select a fund from the universe. The obviously don't.
turns.zh: 但这些基金握着 60% 的资产，那么“70% 的主动型投资者都失败了”这个结论，其实并不准确。它还引出了另一个关于挑选经理（manager selection）的有意思的问题。我们谈论主动管理时，常常好像投资者是从整个基金池里随机挑了一只基金——但他们显然不是这么做的。

turns.en: Assets tend to concentrate in certain managers and in certain firms that doesn't mean investors are always good at selecting managers, they're not. And past performance can attract assets at exactly the wrong time. But it does mean the experience of the average invested dollar can look different from the experience of the average fund.
turns.zh: 资产往往会集中在某些经理、某些公司手里。这并不意味着投资者总是擅长挑经理——他们并不擅长；而且过往业绩可能恰恰在最错误的时间点吸引来资产。但这确实意味着：平均每一块投资出去的钱的体验，可能和平均每只基金的体验并不一样。

turns.en: And that brings me to what may be the biggest problem with the active versus passive debate. We tend to ask whether active management works as though active management or one strategy it isn't. Think about how the different managers I've had on this podcast are. We've talked to managers investing
turns.zh: 这就把我带到了主动 versus 被动（active versus passive）这场辩论里可能是最大的一个问题上。我们总是去问“主动管理行不行得通”，就好像主动管理是同一种策略一样——可它并不是。想想我请上过这档播客的那些经理，彼此有多么不同就知道了。我们聊过投资

turns.en: in large cap growth, value, emerging markets, small and mid cap stocks, global equities, corporate bonds, securitized credit, and a few other areas. The opportunity set is different. The benchmark is different. Market efficiency is different. And the tools available to the managers are different. And so the results tend to be different.
turns.zh: 大盘成长、价值、新兴市场（emerging markets）、中小盘股票、全球股票、公司债（corporate bonds）、证券化信用（securitized credit）以及其他几个领域的经理。他们的机会集（opportunity set）不同，基准不同，市场效率不同，经理手上可用的工具也不同。所以结果往往也不同。

turns.en: And one of the most striking examples from my research has been global bonds. Over the 10 year period I studied, 96% of active global aggregate bond funds beat the Bloomberg Multiverse Index. Compare that with some areas of the equity market where relatively small minority of active managers
turns.zh: 而我的研究里最引人注目的例子之一，就是全球债券。在我研究的那 10 年区间里，96% 的主动型全球综合债券基金（global aggregate bond funds）跑赢了 Bloomberg Multiverse Index。拿这个和股票市场的某些领域比一比——在那些领域里，只有相对很小一部分的主动型经理

turns.en: have beaten their benchmarks over long periods of time. Those aren't small differences. And I don't think the right conclusion is simply that active bond managers are good and active equity managers are bad. I think the more useful question is why the opportunity for active management appears to be so different.
turns.zh: 能在长时间里跑赢它们的基准。这些差异可不是小差异。我并不认为正确的结论就是简简单单的“主动型债券经理行、主动型股票经理不行”。我觉得更有用的问题是：为什么主动管理的机会看起来会如此不同。

turns.en: A bond index isn't constructed like an equity index. Issures that borrow more money can become larger weights on a bond benchmark. Managers can make decisions about duration, credit, sectors, currencies, and positioning along the yield curve. The benchmark itself can create opportunities and constraints that are very different
turns.zh: 债券指数的构建方式和股票指数并不一样。借钱越多的发行人（issuers），在债券基准里的权重可能就越大。经理可以在久期（duration）、信用、行业、货币，以及沿收益率曲线（yield curve）的布局上做决策。基准本身就能创造出与股票基准

turns.en: from an equity benchmark. That's one reason I've become increasingly skeptical whenever I hear someone make a blanket statement that active management works or active management doesn't work. My response is active management where? What kind of manager against what benchmark over what period? And what exactly are we defining as success?
turns.zh: 截然不同的机会和约束。这也是为什么，每当我听到有人一概而论地说“主动管理行得通”或者“主动管理行不通”时，我会越来越持怀疑态度。我的回应是：哪里的主动管理？什么样的经理，对标什么样的基准，在多长的时间段里？而我们究竟把什么定义为成功？

turns.en: Those questions matter. And I think that's probably the biggest thing I've taken away from doing this podcast along with my research. The numbers and the conversations are really answering different questions. My research can tell me which managers beat, how much they beat by what characteristic the winners had,
turns.zh: 这些问题都很关键。我想，这大概就是我做这档播客、再加上我自己的研究，得到的最大收获：数据和对话，其实是在回答不同的问题。我的研究能告诉我哪些经理跑赢了、跑赢了多少、赢家有哪些共同特征、

turns.en: how much risk they took and whether investors actually benefited, but it can't necessarily tell me why a manager made a particular decision. And that's where talking to managers becomes useful. At the same time, listening to a manager describe a thoughtful, disciplined investment process
turns.zh: 他们承担了多少风险、投资者是否真的受益；但它未必能告诉我，一位经理为什么做出某个特定的决策。而这，正是与经理对话变得有用的地方。与此同时，听一位经理描述一套深思熟虑、有纪律的投资流程，

turns.en: can't tell me whether that process actually creates value. That's where the numbers matter. You need both. And if I were trying to identify an active manager today, I don't think I'd start by asking whether they beat the benchmark last year. I'd want to understand what they're actually trying to exploit. Why should this opportunity exist?
turns.zh: 也没法告诉我这套流程是否真的创造了价值。这时候，数据就重要了。你两样都需要。如果今天让我去甄别一位主动管理型经理，我想我不会一上来就问“他去年有没有跑赢基准”。我会想先弄明白：他到底想利用的是什么？这个机会为什么应该存在？

turns.en: Why should this particular management be able to take advantage of it? What does their portfolio look like when their process is working and what does it look like when it's not? How do they know when they're wrong? And then I'd go back to the numbers and ask whether the evidence is consistent with the story
turns.zh: 为什么恰恰是这位经理能够抓住它？当他的流程奏效时，他的组合（portfolio）长什么样；不奏效时，又长什么样？他怎么知道自己错了？然后我会回到数据上，去问：这些证据，是否和他讲给我的故事相符——

turns.en: they're telling me, not whether they outperform every year. No credible investment or active investment process is going to do that. But if a manager tells me their advantage comes from protecting capital when markets fall, I should be able to see some evidence of that. If they tell me they're willing to look different
turns.zh: 而不是问他是不是年年都跑赢。没有任何一个可信的、主动型的投资流程能做到年年跑赢。但如果一位经理告诉我，他的优势在于市场下跌时能保住本金，那我应该能看到一些佐证。如果他告诉我，他愿意让自己的组合看上去

turns.en: from the benchmark, I should be able to see that in the portfolio. And if they tell me valuation is central to their process, their holdings and trading decisions should reflect that. And if they tell me their edge is long-term investing, I want to understand what they actually do when the market tests that patience.
turns.zh: 和基准不一样，那我应该能在组合里看到这一点。如果他告诉我估值是他流程的核心，那他的持仓和交易决策就应该体现出这一点。而如果他告诉我，他的优势是长期投资，我就想弄明白：当市场考验这份耐心的时候，他实际上会怎么做。

turns.en: That's really what I've been trying to get out with inside active, not simply whether active management works, but how it works, where it works, why it might work, and how we can distinguish a repeatable investment process from a good story attached to good performance. We'll get back to our regular conversations
turns.zh: 这其实才是我做 Inside Active 一直想弄清楚的东西——不只是“主动管理行不行得通”，而是它怎么行得通、在哪里行得通、为什么可能行得通，以及我们该怎么把一套可复制的投资流程，和一个“好故事配上了好业绩”区分开来。在接下来的几期里，我们会重新回到

turns.en: with portfolio managers and other industry guests on the next few episodes. But I just want to thank you for listening to Inside Active. If you like the episode, please share it, subscribe, and the review. And if you'd like to see more of our research on the terminal, go to Buy Fun Go for US Fund and Active Research.
turns.zh: 和投资组合经理以及业内其他嘉宾的常规对话。不过在这儿，我想先谢谢你收听 Inside Active。如果你喜欢这一期，请把它分享出去、订阅，并留下一条评价。如果你想在终端（terminal）上看到更多我们的研究，请输入 {FUND GO}，查看 US Fund and Active Research（美国基金与主动管理研究）。
